tldr: When humanoids perform tasks while walking, evaluating candidate actions in latent space based on visual progress toward a goal and body-hand coordination before execution significantly cuts down task failures.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed method. For action candidate prefixes generated by the Action DiT, the system computes visual progress $V_i$ in the V-JEPA feature space and temporal consistency energy $E_i$ to select the best action. During training, action consistency regularization (ACR) reconstructs the initial action, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information.
overview:
When humanoids perform whole-body loco-manipulation tasks—such as carrying a basket and placing it on a table, or loading clothes into a washing machine—they must seamlessly synchronize whole-body locomotion with fine manipulation. However, commands produced by conventional Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often look plausible yet cause fatal timing mismatches, like releasing an object just before it touches the table or dropping clothes before opening a door fully.

To address this, the authors developed action-conditioned latent foresight, a framework that looks ahead and evaluates "what will happen if this action is taken" in latent space before execution. For multiple action candidates proposed by an action generator, the system scores them using two metrics: visual progress, measuring how close the reached visual features are to a subgoal, and temporal consistency, measuring whether body locomotion and hand motions harmonize naturally. The robot then executes only the initial steps of the top-scoring action and replans from the next observation.

Evaluated on 10 tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark SIMPLE and 7 tasks on a real humanoid (Unitree G1), the method achieved an average success rate of 89.7% in simulation (surpassing strong baselines like DiT4DiT at 82.0% and $\Psi_0$ at 73.7%). On the real robot, it reached 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations. Looking ahead to select actions alongside consistency regularization proved to dramatically boost success in complex coordinated tasks.
contributions: Proposed action-conditioned latent foresight, which pre-evaluates and selects candidate sequences of whole-body motion and hand commands using predicted visual progress in latent space and a learned temporal prior.

Developed action consistency regularization (ACR), a training-time regularization that reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, preventing the latent predictor from losing fine-grained action details.

Demonstrated significant improvements in task success rates over state-of-the-art VLA baselines across 10 simulation tasks and 7 real-robot tasks on a Unitree G1 (including unseen object configurations).

sections.heading: Why is humanoid loco-manipulation so prone to failure?
sections.summary: Everyday humanoid tasks require tight coordination between body locomotion and hand manipulation, where small timing errors can drop objects. This paper introduces action-conditioned latent foresight to evaluate and filter generated action candidates in latent space before execution.
sections.details:
When a humanoid tackles daily chores like tidying up or doing laundry, it must coordinate whole-body locomotion and fine manipulation with high precision. For instance, in a task where the robot carries a basket and places it on a desk, it must maintain a firm grasp until the basket fully settles on the surface. Releasing the grasp even slightly too early drops the basket to the floor, failing the task.

While recent VLA models can generate actions directly from images and language, it remains difficult to foresee which sampled action sequence among multiple candidates will reliably finish the task. Most existing world–action models (WAMs) only use future prediction as an auxiliary feature extractor during training. They do not fully leverage these models to compare and filter multiple generated action candidates at test time.

Two evaluation axes are critical here: "how much closer will this action bring the robot to the goal (visual progress)" and "do the locomotion and hand actions coordinate naturally without conflicting across time (temporal consistency)?" This work builds a framework that evaluates both criteria rapidly in latent feature space, selecting the best action for receding-horizon execution.

sections.heading: From VLAs and world models to pre-execution evaluation
sections.summary: This section reviews humanoid VLAs, world models, and latent planning. While standard world models mainly serve as conditioning inputs for generation, the proposed method acts as a pre-execution verifier to filter multiple generated action sequences.
sections.details:
The authors categorize related work into three main directions:

### Humanoid VLAs and World–Action Models (WAMs)
Extending VLAs like OpenVLA to humanoids has yielded models like $\Psi_0$, which relies on egocentric pretraining, and WholeBodyVLA, which learns latent actions from videos. WAMs that tie video prediction to action generation (such as DreamZero, DiT4DiT, and MotionWAM) have also emerged. However, they use predicted features as inputs to generate actions, lacking a mechanism to compare and select among candidate outputs at test time.

### Action-Supervised Learning for Latent Prediction
In world models like JEPA (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture) that forecast the future in latent space, predicting state transitions conditioned on actions is an active area. While latent spaces effectively discard task-irrelevant background noise, they risk overlooking subtle differences in hand actions. This work introduces action consistency regularization, which reconstructs the original action from predicted latent feature changes to ensure the predictor retains action-relevant information.

### Temporal Action Priors and Sequence Scoring
To preserve action smoothness and naturalness, past approaches used fixed smoothing penalties or high-level ratings from VLMs. However, simple smoothing falls short for humanoids, where locomotion and manipulation closely depend on each other. This work introduces a GRU-based joint temporal prior that learns the mutual dependencies between body motion and hand commands, detecting when candidate sequences break down.

sections.heading: Looking ahead before choosing: How latent foresight works
sections.summary: For multiple action sequences proposed by the action generator, an endpoint predictor scores visual progress toward subgoals while a joint temporal prior evaluates body-hand coordination. The system executes only the first step of the best sequence in an MPC loop, boosted by ACR during training.
sections.details:
The pipeline consists of three stages: candidate generation, latent evaluation, and execution/replanning (Figure F2).

### III-A Problem Formulation and Receding-Horizon Evaluation
From an observation image $o_t$, language instruction $\ell$, and proprioceptive state $s_t$, the action generator samples $N$ command sequences $A_t^{(i)}$ of length $H$. Each command includes a locomotion component $m_k$ and a hand target $u_k$. For a prefix $B_t^{(i)}$ of horizon $h$ ($2 \le h \le H$), the system computes an overall score $V_i - \beta E_i$ from visual progress $V_i$ and temporal consistency energy $E_i$. The robot executes only the first $K$ steps of the top-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation in a receding-horizon fashion.

### III-B Action Generation
A Qwen3-VL-2B model encodes images and language, feeding tokens to an Action DiT (Diffusion Transformer). A flow-matching velocity prediction head integrates numerically from initial noise to generate the $N$ command sequences.

### III-C Action-Conditioned Endpoint Dynamics
A frozen V-JEPA 2.1 (ViT-L/16) backbone, fine-tuned on real in-home G1 teleoperation data (HIW-500, over 500 hours), serves as the visual feature extractor. Command sequences are tokenized by an encoder $C_\eta$, added to predicted tokens from the VLM, and fed into an endpoint predictor. This directly estimates the predicted feature $\widehat{\mathbf{f}}_{t+h}$ reached after $h$ steps from the current image feature $\mathbf{f}_t$ and candidate action $B$. Visual progress $V_i$ is measured by how much closer this brings the robot to demonstration-derived ordered subgoal features $z_g$ in terms of cosine distance.

### III-D Joint Temporal Prior
Locomotion and manipulation are not independent; they exhibit strong temporal correlations, such as reaching while walking or pulling back only after coming to a stop. The authors train a shared GRU on state $s_t$ and past command history to predict the next joint whole-body and hand command. The candidate sequence's deviation from this prior (squared prediction error) forms the energy penalty $E_i$.

### III-E Action Consistency Regularization (ACR)
To prevent mode collapse where the predictor ignores action differences, an inverse action decoder $D_\psi$ is added during training only. It reconstructs the first demonstrated command $a_{t,0}$ from both observed feature change $\Delta z$ and predicted feature change $\Delta \hat{z}$. Gradients from this reconstruction backpropagate into the predictor, forcing its latent predictions to preserve action-specific information.

captions.F2: Model architecture of the proposed method. Multiple sequences are generated by the Action DiT (top left), scored by V-JEPA, the endpoint predictor, and the joint temporal prior (top right), and regularized during training via the inverse action decoder for action consistency (bottom).

sections.heading: Testing in sim and real: Can it handle unseen object layouts?
sections.summary: Evaluated across 10 SIMPLE simulation tasks and 7 real-robot tasks on a Unitree G1, the method achieved 89.7% average success in simulation and 85.7% on the real robot (65.7% under unseen setups), outperforming prior VLAs. Ablations confirmed the value of both ACR and the joint prior.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated complex manipulation tasks requiring locomotion in both simulation and the real world.

### IV-A Experimental Setup
Simulation used 10 tasks from the loco-manipulation benchmark SIMPLE (Figure F3). Each task was evaluated across 10 trials under three randomization levels (L0/L1/L2) covering backgrounds, lighting, and initial poses. Real-robot experiments used a Unitree G1 on 7 tasks, such as loading clothes into a washing machine and watering plants with a can. Real tests included standard conditions as well as unseen configurations with object types, positions, and orientations not seen in demonstrations.

### IV-B Task Success Rates
- **Simulation**: The method achieved an average success rate of 89.7% across 10 tasks, significantly outperforming DiT4DiT (82.0%), $\Psi_0$ (73.7%), and VLA-JEPA (49.0%).
- **Real Robot**: It reached 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% in unseen configurations. The strongest baseline, GR00T N1.7, achieved only 70.0% and 48.6%, respectively. In "Load Washer" specifically, GR00T N1.7 succeeded in only 2/10 trials, while the proposed method scored 10/10. GR00T frequently dropped the clothes while walking or let go right in front of the drum.

### IV-C Qualitative Results and Generalization
The robot adapted flexibly when watering can spouts faced the wrong way or shirts were placed on the left (Figure F4). Even when demonstrations only showed right-handed grasps, the robot naturally switched to its left hand when dictated by the layout and completed the task. This emergent left-handed grasping without demonstrations was a notable highlight.

### IV-D Data Efficiency and Failure Analysis
When reducing demonstrations to 25, 50, and 100 trajectories, the method consistently showed higher robustness than $\Psi_0$ (84.0% vs. 56.7% at 100 demos). Main failure modes (Figure F6) included failing to rotate a faucet handle fully (OpenFaucet), hesitating to drop trash when the bin lid opened only halfway (Dispose of Trash), and dropping a soft plush toy (Collect Toy with Cart).

### IV-F Ablation Studies
Ablations on four challenging simulation tasks verified each design choice:
- **Action Consistency Regularization (ACR)**: Disabling ACR dropped the success rate from 65.8% to 55.0% (a 10.8-point drop), showing that preserving action details in the predictor is essential.
- **Temporal Prior Design**: The proposed Joint Prior reached 80.8%. This clearly surpassed using visual progress alone (65.8%), fixed smoothing penalties (67.5%–70.0%), and a Factorized Prior predicting locomotion and hands separately (71.6%), highlighting the need to model body-hand cross-dependencies.

### IV-G Inference Cost
The model uses less than half the GPU memory of DiT4DiT and Fast-WAM while running faster. On an onboard Jetson Orin NX (16GB), it ran stably using 12.84 GB of memory at 0.73 Hz.

sections.heading: Conclusions and next steps: Expanding to contact and object state
sections.summary: This work advances humanoid loco-manipulation by scoring visual progress and temporal consistency in latent space. Future directions include incorporating contact-state awareness and evaluating temporal consistency across multiple command chunks.
sections.details:
This paper introduced action-conditioned latent foresight to evaluate and filter generated action sequences prior to execution. Achieving 89.7% in simulation and 85.7% on a real robot (65.7% in unseen setups), the results show that action consistency regularization (ACR) and a joint temporal prior play decisive roles in boosting success.

However, failure modes remain around incomplete articulation of mechanisms (like faucets or pedal trash bins) and dropping deformable objects. In addition, computing visual scores relies on demonstration-derived subgoal sequences, and the onboard Jetson inference speed remains at 0.73 Hz.

The authors outline future work to include physical contact information and fine-grained object state changes into the latent dynamics, as well as extending temporal consistency evaluation across multiple consecutive command chunks rather than just within a single chunk.

takeaways: Filtering VLA action candidates through latent pre-execution evaluation dramatically boosts success rates in coordinated loco-manipulation tasks.
When building latent predictive models, regularizing them to reconstruct the initial action from feature changes (ACR) prevents mode collapse where the model ignores subtle action differences.
Humanoid control benefits heavily from modeling the mutual dependencies between body locomotion and hand motions (joint temporal prior) rather than smoothing them independently.
Even simple metrics like latent feature distance to subgoal images act as powerful closed-loop trajectory verifiers when paired with a temporal consistency score.
limitations: Requires extracting temporally ordered subgoal images from successful human demonstrations beforehand, making it difficult to apply directly to zero-shot tasks or open-ended exploration.
Latent features alone sometimes struggle to capture millimeter-level contacts and subtle physical interactions with articulated mechanisms, such as turning faucets or stepping on pedal bins.
Running onboard a Jetson Orin NX yields an inference rate of around 0.73 Hz (about once every 1.37 seconds), which remains challenging for real-time reactive corrections against sudden disturbances.
